content_voiceover: This slide covers AML maintenance therapy in the post-transplant setting, and the key message up front is that no drug is currently FDA approved here. For patients without allo-HSCT, options mirror the prior slide, HMA maintenance with azacitidine, azacitidine plus venetoclax from the VIALE-T trial, or Onureg being studied in the AMADEUS trial. But there's an important pitfall to recognize, patients with the highest risk disease, meaning active graft versus host disease or significant cytopenias, are often unable to tolerate maintenance therapy after transplant, and those are exactly the patients destined for worse outcomes anyway. That selection bias can artificially inflate the apparent benefit of post-HSCT maintenance in observational analyses. For patients who do proceed to allo-HSCT, FLT3 inhibitor maintenance has the most evidence, quizartinib from the QuANTUM-R and QuANTUM-First trials showing an overall survival benefit, sorafenib showing relapse free survival and reduced relapse rate benefits across two separate trials, and gilteritinib data published in Lancet Hematology in 2024.
keypoints: No FDA-approved maintenance therapy currently exists in the post-HSCT setting
Non-transplant options: azacitidine, azacitidine plus venetoclax, Onureg
Post-HSCT options for FLT3-mutated disease: quizartinib, sorafenib, gilteritinib
Pitfall: sickest post-HSCT patients often can't tolerate maintenance, biasing benefit estimates
keypoint_voiceover: Two things to hold onto here. First, unlike the non-transplant setting, nothing is FDA approved for maintenance after allo-HSCT yet, though FLT3 inhibitors like quizartinib, sorafenib, and gilteritinib have the strongest supporting data for FLT3 mutated patients. Second, watch for the selection bias pitfall, patients too sick from graft versus host disease or cytopenias to receive maintenance are also the ones most likely to relapse, which can make maintenance look more effective than it truly is.
